Profuse

pruh-FYOOSS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Profuse is exuberantly plentiful.

The gardener's rosebushes produced profuse blooms every June.

Worked Example

He offered profuse apologies to the entire staff after the scheduling error.

This wasn't a single quick apology -- it was an outpouring of many, many apologies, which is exactly profuse.

How Profuse Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

plentiful

plentiful: existing in large quantities

generous

generous: large and freely given in quantity

Antonyms

meager

meager: small in amount and lacking in quantity

How Strong Is It? — enough → profuse → overflowing

enough vs. profuse

enough vs. profuse: Having enough simply means the need is met; profuse suggests an almost overflowing, lavish supply.

overflowing vs. profuse

overflowing vs. profuse: Profuse describes a generous supply; overflowing suggests that supply has exceeded its limits entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: forth (Latin)

root — fuse

root — fuse: to pour (Latin (fundere))

Put it together

Put it together: Profuse comes from Latin pro- ('forth') + fundere ('to pour') -- literally 'poured forth,' describing something flowing out generously.

Use the root in a new word: refuse

Use the root in a new word: refuse: The same fundere root gives us refuse (re- 'back' + fundere, originally 'to pour back,' i.e. reject) and confuse (con- 'together' + fundere, 'to pour together').

Root Check

Word Choice

Profuse most often describes something flowing or growing plentifully -- sweat, apologies, blossoms, thanks -- always with a positive or at least mild, generous connotation.
